title: Rewrite emails for tone & clarity
blurb: Paste a draft and say "make this more direct" or "soften this — we need to keep the relationship warm." Get a polished version in seconds.
detail: You know that email you wrote at 4:55pm on a Friday? The one that's technically accurate but sounds like it was typed by someone who just lost an argument? Claude fixes that. Paste your draft, describe the vibe you're going for — "professional but not cold," "apologetic without groveling," "direct without sounding like a jerk" — and it rewrites it. You still sign it. It just doesn't sound like a war memo anymore.
prompt: Here's my draft. Make it firmer but keep it professional — we need to push back on the timeline without blowing up the relationship.

title: Prep for meetings fast
blurb: Share an agenda or background doc and ask Claude to prep you with likely questions, key talking points, or a one-page brief. Walk in ready.
detail: Nobody reads the pre-read. But you should at least know what's in it. Drop the agenda, the deck, or the background doc into Chat and ask Claude to brief you in plain English: what's being decided, where the likely tension is, what questions might come your way, and what you should probably say. Five minutes before walking in. Way better than scanning slides in the elevator.
prompt: Here's the agenda for Thursday's supplier review. What should I be ready for, and what are the two or three things I should push on?

title: Decode acronyms & internal jargon
blurb: New to Aptera or just hit a TLA you don't recognize? Ask Claude. Add context and it'll explain the concept, not just the letters.
detail: Every company develops a dialect. Aptera's no different. ECR, BOM, DVP, NCR, GL, PO, SOX — second nature to some, total gibberish to others. Ask Claude what something means and it won't just spit out the acronym expansion. It'll explain the concept, why it matters, and how it fits into the workflow. Context included, no side-eye for asking.
prompt: What's a DVP&R and why does everyone keep asking if the one for the canopy is 'locked'?

title: Translate technical docs for executives
blurb: Hand Claude a dense engineering write-up and ask for the version your VP will actually read — short, plain, and decision-focused.
detail: Engineers write for engineers. Executives read for decisions. Those are two different languages, and the translation usually falls to whoever's least busy — which is nobody. Claude bridges the gap. Paste the test report, the design rationale, or the post-mortem and ask for an exec summary: what happened, why it matters, what it costs, and what you need from leadership. It strips the acronyms, kills the passive voice, leads with the bottom line, and keeps it to half a page. You keep the technical truth; you just lose the parts that make a CFO's eyes glaze over. Tell it the audience and the ask, and you'll get something you can paste straight into an email or a board slide without apologizing for the length.
prompt: Here's our thermal validation report on the solar array. Write a half-page summary for our exec team: what we found, the risk to the launch timeline, the cost impact, and the one decision we need from them.

title: Draft job descriptions & interview questions
blurb: Describe the role in a sentence or two and get a real job description plus a structured interview kit — competencies, questions, and what good answers sound like.
detail: Hiring is slow partly because the writing is annoying. A good job description has to sell the role, set honest expectations, and not read like every other listing on the internet. Tell Claude the title, the team, the must-haves, and the vibe you're after, and it drafts a description that sounds like Aptera — mission-forward, specific, not a wall of boilerplate. Then ask for the interview kit: behavioral and technical questions mapped to the competencies that actually matter, plus a quick rubric for what a strong, average, and weak answer looks like so your panel grades the same way. It won't make the hire for you. It just means you stop reusing the same tired template from 2019 and start interviewing with a plan.
prompt: We're hiring a manufacturing process engineer for the composites line. Draft a job description in Aptera's voice, then give me 8 interview questions — mix of behavioral and technical — with a short rubric for what a strong answer looks like.

title: Draft vendor communications
blurb: Dispute an invoice, request payment terms, or follow up on a PO — describe the situation and Claude drafts a professional email you can send (or tweak).
detail: Vendor emails are a diplomatic art. Too aggressive and you damage a relationship you might need. Too soft and nothing happens. Claude threads the needle: describe the situation — late invoice, disputed charge, payment terms you need to push — and it drafts something firm, professional, and unlikely to generate a passive-aggressive reply. Edit what you want. Send it with confidence.
prompt: Our vendor submitted an invoice 40% over the agreed PO amount and hasn't responded to our last two emails. Draft something serious that still keeps the door open.

title: Explain GL coding questions
blurb: Not sure how to code an unusual expense? Describe it and ask. Claude walks through the logic so you can make the call confidently.
detail: GL coding is one of those things where the answer is obvious once you know the rules and maddening until you do. Is this software subscription a prepaid or an expense? Is this a capital purchase or an operating cost? Does this warranty extend the asset life? Claude knows the accounting logic and can walk you through the reasoning — so you make the call with confidence, not a coin flip.
prompt: We bought a forklift attachment for $12k that'll last 7 years. Do we capitalize this or expense it? Walk me through the reasoning.

title: Summarize contracts & agreements
blurb: Paste in a contract section and ask for a plain-English summary of obligations, payment terms, or risk clauses. Faster than re-reading the whole thing.
detail: Legal contracts are written by lawyers for lawyers. The indemnification clause is on page 31, buried in a paragraph that starts with "Notwithstanding." Claude reads it so you don't have to dig through all of it. Paste the relevant section and ask for a plain-English breakdown: what we're on the hook for, when payment triggers, what the escape clauses are, what looks one-sided. Not legal advice — but a much better starting point than squinting at 11-point font.
prompt: Summarize the payment terms and termination clause in this vendor agreement. Flag anything that looks unusual or heavily one-sided.

title: Brainstorm campaign names
blurb: Give Claude the product angle, target audience, and vibe. Get 15 name ideas in 30 seconds. Push it harder: "more irreverent," "more premium," "pun-based."
detail: The best campaign names don't come from a committee. They come from one person having an idea at the right moment — and now that person has an AI assistant that's read basically everything. Give Claude the product story, the audience, the energy you're going for. Get 15–20 name concepts in under a minute. Then push it: "more audacious," "something a little weird," "what would Apple call this?" The first round is a warm-up. The second and third rounds are where it gets interesting.
prompt: We're launching a campaign around Aptera's solar panel integration. Audience: EV-curious but not tech-obsessed. Give me 15 campaign names — some serious, some playful, a couple that are borderline too much.

title: Rewrite copy for different tones
blurb: Technical copy → excited consumer copy. Formal press release → punchy social caption. Feed Claude the original and the target tone and watch it transform.
detail: The same fact can be boring or electric depending on how it's framed. "The vehicle charges while parked outdoors" is correct. "Your commute is already paid for — by the sun" is a campaign. Claude can shift register from technical to emotional, from formal to casual, from press release to tweet. Feed it the source copy and the destination tone. It doesn't just swap words — it rethinks the angle.
prompt: Here's a paragraph from our engineering spec sheet. Rewrite it for a general consumer audience — excited, not technical, punchy enough for a landing page hero section.

title: Generate social post variations
blurb: Write one solid post and ask Claude to give you 5 variations: different hooks, lengths, or angles for different platforms. A/B test without the effort.
detail: You have one good idea. You need it in five formats for three platforms. Claude handles the multiplication. Write one solid post — the one that captures the real message — and ask for variations: different hooks, different lengths, different angles (humor vs. authority vs. curiosity). You get an A/B test's worth of options without an A/B test's worth of effort. Pick the three that feel right. Kill the rest.
prompt: Here's my LinkedIn post about our range milestone. Give me 5 variations — one shorter, one with a question hook, one more data-driven, one more emotional, and one bold enough that I might not use it.

title: Explain error messages
blurb: Paste the stack trace and a snippet of context. Claude explains what actually went wrong and offers likely causes — faster than a Stack Overflow deep-dive.
detail: Stack traces were designed by engineers for engineers who enjoy pain. A wall of text that tells you "NullPointerException at line 847" is technically useful and practically useless. Claude doesn't just decode the message — it tells you what likely caused it, which part of your code is probably responsible, what to check first, and what the common pitfall is. It's like having a senior engineer look over your shoulder, except they never sigh audibly.
prompt: Here's a stack trace from our CI run. The error appears intermittent. Tell me what actually went wrong and the two most likely root causes.

title: Rubber-duck design decisions
blurb: Talk through an architecture choice out loud. Claude asks the clarifying questions your rubber duck can't, and pushes back on assumptions — usefully.
detail: The rubber duck debugging method works because articulating a problem forces clarity. Claude is a rubber duck that talks back — and knows a lot of computer science. Explain your architecture decision, your tradeoff, your nagging doubt about the data model. Claude will ask the clarifying questions that expose what you haven't fully worked out, offer counter-considerations, and help you think through the consequences. It won't make the decision for you. It'll make sure you've actually thought it through.
prompt: I'm deciding between a JSONB column in Postgres vs. a proper normalized schema for this data. Here's the access pattern. What am I not thinking about?

title: Quick regex / syntax help
blurb: "Write a regex that matches ISO dates but not times." Done. Ask it to explain the pattern too so you actually understand what you're shipping.
detail: Life is too short to remember regex syntax. Claude remembers regex syntax so you don't have to. Describe the pattern in plain English — "match a US phone number with or without dashes," "find all Confluence URLs in this text," "capture the version number from these filenames" — and Claude hands you the expression, explains every piece of it, and flags edge cases you probably didn't consider. Ask it to test the regex against your actual examples while you're at it.
prompt: Write a regex that matches semantic version strings like 1.0.0 and 2.14.3-beta but not '1.0' or 'v2'. Explain each part.

title: Summarize supplier spec sheets
blurb: Paste the dense technical text from a supplier datasheet. Ask Claude to pull out the specs that actually matter for your process in plain language.
detail: Supplier datasheets come in 40 pages of dense technical content, 8 of which actually matter to you. Claude reads the whole thing so you can ask the right questions. Paste the spec sheet text and tell Claude what you actually need to know: operating ranges, material compatibility, dimensional tolerances, shelf life, whatever. It pulls the signal out of the noise and delivers it in language you can use.
prompt: Here's the datasheet for the adhesive we're evaluating. Our cure temp is 85°C. Does this product support that, and what are the key storage and pot-life considerations?

title: Explain process standards
blurb: Need a quick primer on IPC standards, incoming inspection criteria, or a manufacturing process you're less familiar with? Ask Claude for the key points.
detail: Process standards exist to capture institutional knowledge — which means they're often dense, assume existing expertise, and don't explain why anything works the way it does. Claude bridges the gap. Ask about IPC acceptance criteria, ISO 9001 requirements, PFMEA methodology, first article inspection protocols — whatever you're trying to get up to speed on. It explains the what, the why, and how it applies to your situation. Background context without a three-day course.
prompt: Explain what a Control Plan is, how it relates to the PFMEA, and what a manufacturing engineer needs to do to maintain one correctly.

title: Draft non-conformance notes
blurb: Describe the defect and Claude drafts a clear, structured NCR narrative — root cause, disposition, corrective action stubs. Start from something, not nothing.
detail: NCRs need to be clear, factual, and structured — and they're almost always written right after something went wrong, which is the worst time to write clearly. Claude takes the pressure off. Describe the defect, the discovery point, the suspected cause, and what you know so far. Claude drafts a structured NCR narrative: defect description, root cause hypothesis, disposition recommendation, corrective action placeholders. You fill in the facts. It handles the structure.
prompt: Dimensional non-conformance on a batch of brackets — hole position is 0.4mm out of spec, found at incoming inspection. Draft an NCR with what we know so far.

title: Explain CATIA macro parameters
blurb: Paste a VBA macro snippet and ask Claude what each parameter does. Get an explanation you can actually use — no hunting through decade-old forum posts.
detail: CATIA VBA macros look like they were written in a language that predates the internet, because they basically were. The documentation is thin, the forums are ancient, and half the parameter names are cryptic abbreviations. Paste the macro snippet into Claude and ask what each parameter does, what the valid values are, and what breaks if you change something. You get an explanation you can act on — no 2009 forum thread required.
prompt: Here's a VBA macro that exports parts to STEP. I don't understand what AxisSystemType controls or what the valid values are. Explain it.

title: Draft change request descriptions
blurb: Tell Claude what changed geometrically and why. It drafts a clear ECR/ECO description that actually communicates the intent to downstream teams.
detail: Engineering changes need to communicate clearly across mechanical, manufacturing, and supply chain — three groups with different mental models of the same hardware. Claude helps translate. Describe the change: what moved, what dimension changed, what tolerance tightened, and why. Claude drafts a description that covers the technical delta, the functional reason, and the downstream impact — in language that actually makes sense to whoever has to approve and implement it.
prompt: The front fascia mounting bracket moved 3mm inboard to clear the new sensor housing. Draft an ECR description covering what changed, why, and which teams need to review it.

title: Decode GD&T callouts
blurb: Describe a feature control frame and Claude explains what it means functionally — what it allows, what it prohibits, and how a CMM would check it.
detail: GD&T is a precise language for describing geometric requirements — and like any precise language, it takes years to become fluent. Claude can parse any feature control frame and explain what it actually requires: what datum references mean functionally, how the tolerance zone is defined in 3D space, whether material condition modifiers apply, and how a CMM would be set up to verify it. Great for sanity-checking your own callouts or decoding someone else's.
prompt: Explain this callout: ⌀0.2 Ⓜ A B C. What does it mean in plain English and how would you verify it on a CMM?

title: PDF → Confluence in one shot
blurb: Share a PDF report or meeting transcript. Claude summarizes it, pulls key decisions and action items, and pushes a structured page directly to Confluence — formatted and ready.
detail: Here's the workflow Co-Work replaces: someone takes notes in a meeting, emails them around, someone else creates a Confluence page, pastes things in the wrong order, and the doc sits unformatted for two weeks. Co-Work short-circuits all of it. Drop the PDF, the transcript, or the notes. Tell it which Confluence space and parent page to use. It reads the content, structures it sensibly, writes proper headings and sections, and creates the page. You review it. Done.
prompt: Here's the PDF from last week's supplier review. Create a Confluence page in the Manufacturing space with a summary, key decisions, and action items listed with owners.

title: Weekly status reports from notes
blurb: Dump your rough notes from the week. Claude structures them into a proper weekly status report — wins, blockers, next steps — and posts it where your team expects it.
detail: Status reports are useful artifacts. They're also the thing everyone does last, in 15 minutes, poorly, on Friday afternoon. Co-Work changes the equation: give it your rough notes, Slack threads, or a voice memo transcript. It structures them into a real status report — achievements, blockers, what's coming next, who owns what — and publishes it to Confluence before you leave for the weekend. Future-you will appreciate past-you's low effort.
prompt: Here are my notes from this week. Create a status report in Confluence with sections for completed, in-progress, blocked, and next week. Keep it concise.

title: Teams meeting → Confluence minutes
blurb: Drop your Teams transcript and run the Meeting Minutes skill. Claude confirms attendees, infers the meeting title, extracts decisions and action items, and publishes structured minutes to Confluence.
detail: Every Teams meeting ends with a transcript and the quiet understanding that nobody is going to do anything with it. This skill changes that. Upload the .vtt or .txt transcript file, run the Meeting Minutes skill, and Claude takes it from there: it parses the speakers, cleans up transcription artifacts, and asks you to confirm the attendee list (because people in the conference room don't show up as named speakers). Once confirmed, it extracts key decisions, open questions, and action items — then publishes a properly formatted Confluence page and creates Jira tasks for each action item, linked back to the minutes. From "we should do something with this" to "it's already done" in about two minutes.
prompt: Here's the transcript from this morning's supplier review. Run the Meeting Minutes skill and post the notes to Confluence.

title: Pull AP aging from Ramp
blurb: Ask Claude to pull current outstanding payables from Ramp, flag anything past due, and drop the summary into a Confluence page — without opening a single export dialog.
detail: AP aging reports shouldn't require opening five tabs, running an export, cleaning the data, and formatting a summary. With Co-Work connected to Ramp, it doesn't. Ask Claude to pull the current outstanding payables, bucket them by aging category, flag anything past-due or approaching terms, and write a summary you can bring to a meeting or drop into an email. From question to report: one conversation.
prompt: Pull our current AP aging from Ramp. Show me what's current, 30-60 days, and over 60. Flag anything from vendors we have active projects with.

title: Expense report cleanup via Ramp
blurb: Ask Claude to scan Ramp for transactions missing receipts or memos, then draft the nudges to chase them down before close.
detail: Month-end close has a recurring villain: the transaction with no receipt and a memo that just says "stuff." Tracking those down by hand means cross-referencing reports, pinging people in Slack, and re-pinging the same three offenders every single month. Co-Work, connected to Ramp, does the legwork. Ask it to pull every transaction missing a receipt or a coding memo, group them by cardholder, and surface the dollar amounts and dates so you know what's material. Then have it draft the chase-down messages — polite the first time, slightly less polite by the third — ready for you to send. It can also flag transactions where the memo doesn't match the merchant category, which is usually where the interesting questions hide. You still make the calls; Claude just makes sure you're not the one playing receipt detective at 9pm on the last day of the month.
prompt: Pull all Ramp transactions from last month that are missing a receipt or a memo. Group them by cardholder with dollar amounts, and draft a friendly reminder message for each person listing exactly which transactions they still owe.

title: Draft variance analyses
blurb: Feed Claude your actuals vs. budget data. It identifies the significant variances, drafts explanatory narratives for each, and formats everything into a review-ready document.
detail: Variance analysis is part math, part storytelling. The math is easy. The storytelling — explaining why opex came in 18% over budget in a way that's accurate, contextual, and doesn't make anyone look bad — is harder. Give Claude the actuals and budget, call out the significant variances, and it drafts the narrative: what drove the variance, whether it's timing vs. structural, what the outlook implications are. You validate the facts. Claude handles the prose.
prompt: Here are our Q2 actuals vs. budget by department. The biggest variances are in R&D (over) and G&A (under). Draft a variance analysis narrative I can use in the CFO deck.

title: Budget summary docs in Confluence
blurb: Provide raw budget data and Claude builds a structured, properly linked Confluence page — department rollups, charts described in prose, exec summary up top.
detail: A budget summary that lives in a spreadsheet is a document nobody reads. Co-Work takes that data and turns it into a properly structured Confluence page: exec summary up top, department breakdowns in sections, key assumptions called out, variance notes where they exist. The kind of page you'd actually send to a VP and not be embarrassed by. Not a data dump — a document.
prompt: Here's our Q3 budget rollup by department. Build a Confluence page in the Finance space with an executive summary, per-department sections with commentary, and a risks and assumptions section.

title: Research competitors & synthesize
blurb: Give Claude a list of competitors and a research angle. It pulls publicly available information, synthesizes findings, and produces a structured competitive brief — no tab juggling required.
detail: Competitive research at most companies means one person spending two hours with 12 tabs open, producing a doc that's 70% screenshots and 30% observations with no clear so-what. Co-Work does it differently: give Claude a list of competitors and the questions you need answered — pricing, messaging angles, product claims, what's changed recently — and it synthesizes a structured brief you can actually act on. No tabs. No screenshots. Just insight.
prompt: Research how our top three solar EV competitors are positioning their solar charging feature in public marketing. Summarize the key messaging differences and flag any claims that seem aggressive.

title: Build campaign brief docs
blurb: Start from a few bullet points. Claude expands them into a full creative brief — target audience, messaging pillars, channel strategy, success metrics — and saves it to Confluence.
detail: A campaign brief that lives only in someone's head is a liability. Co-Work takes the idea out of your head and into a structured document that can be handed off. Start with bullets — audience, goal, key message, channels, dates. Claude expands them into a full brief with target audience persona, messaging hierarchy, channel strategy, success metrics, and open questions — then saves it to Confluence so your team can comment and align before anyone writes a single word of copy.
prompt: I want to build a brief for our launch campaign around the 1,000-mile range milestone. Audience: long-distance EV buyers. Goal: email signups. Build the brief and save it to the Marketing Confluence space.

title: Create content calendars
blurb: Tell Claude your campaign dates, themes, and channels. It builds a structured content calendar with post topics, formats, and timing — delivered as a shareable Confluence table.
detail: Content calendars are deceptively hard. Not because the strategy is complicated, but because translating "we want to be active on LinkedIn this quarter" into 12 specific posts with dates, formats, topics, and owners is just a lot of work. Co-Work makes it mechanical: give Claude your themes, posting cadence, and channels. It builds a full calendar — dates, topics, format per platform, content angle — structured as a Confluence table ready to share with the whole team.
prompt: Build a 6-week content calendar for LinkedIn and Instagram around Aptera's solar technology. 3 posts per week. Mix of educational, behind-the-scenes, and product-focused. Output as a Confluence table.

title: Analyze open Jira issues
blurb: Point Claude at your Jira project. It reads open tickets, identifies clusters of related issues, flags stale work, and produces a triage summary — useful before sprint planning.
detail: Jira is where good intentions go to age. Open issues accumulate, duplicates multiply, stale tickets from two sprints ago linger at the top of the backlog. Co-Work reads your actual Jira project and does real triage: it identifies clusters of related issues, flags things that haven't moved in 30+ days, spots duplicate descriptions, and produces a summary that's actually useful for a sprint planning conversation. The pre-work before the pre-work — done automatically.
prompt: Read the open issues in our FIRMWARE Jira project. Identify clusters of related bugs, flag anything open more than 45 days without an update, and give me a one-page triage summary.

title: Groom the Jira backlog
blurb: Let Claude do the unglamorous backlog hygiene: find duplicates, flag stale tickets, and propose a re-prioritization you can approve in one pass.
detail: Backlog grooming is the chore everyone agrees is important and nobody volunteers for. So the backlog grows a second head, then a third, and eventually nobody trusts it. Point Co-Work at your Jira project — say the OI Odoo Implementation project — and ask it to do a real grooming pass. It reads every open ticket, spots likely duplicates (two people filed the same bug with different words), flags anything that's gone quiet for 30+ days, and notices tickets missing a priority, an assignee, or an acceptance criterion. Then it proposes changes: merge these two, close this stale one, bump that blocker up, and de-prioritize the nice-to-have nobody's touched since the kickoff. Crucially, it proposes — you approve. Walk through its suggestions, accept the obvious ones, override the rest, and your backlog goes from archaeological dig site to something you'd actually plan a sprint from.
prompt: Go through the open tickets in our OI Jira project. Find likely duplicates, flag anything untouched for 30+ days, list tickets missing a priority or assignee, and propose a re-prioritized backlog for me to review and approve.

title: Create sprint planning docs
blurb: Share your backlog priorities. Claude drafts a sprint plan with capacity notes, ticket breakdowns, and risk flags — then posts it to Confluence for async review before the planning call.
detail: Sprint planning meetings are better when there's a shared artifact to react to instead of a blank whiteboard. Co-Work produces that artifact: feed it your prioritized backlog, team capacity, and any known dependencies. It drafts a sprint plan — which tickets are in, rough effort stacking against capacity, any obvious risks — and posts it to Confluence for async review before the meeting. Your planning call becomes a refinement conversation instead of a starting-from-scratch one.
prompt: We have 8 engineers with ~40 story points this sprint. Here's our prioritized backlog. Draft a proposed sprint plan with rationale, flag dependencies, and post it to our Engineering Confluence space.

title: Draft technical specs
blurb: Describe a feature or system change. Claude drafts a full technical spec — problem statement, proposed solution, API surface, open questions — and creates the Confluence page ready for comment.
detail: A technical spec exists so that "what we agreed to build" is written down before "what we actually built" diverges from it. Co-Work makes writing specs not terrible. Describe the feature: the problem it solves, the proposed approach, the API surface, the open questions. Claude drafts a proper spec — problem statement, proposed solution, alternatives considered, technical notes, open questions — and creates the Confluence page ready for comment. First draft in under a minute.
prompt: We're building a telemetry ingestion service that receives CAN bus data and stores it in our data warehouse. Draft a technical spec with problem statement, proposed architecture, API contract, and open questions.

title: Transcripts → Confluence + Jira
blurb: Paste a meeting transcript. Claude extracts decisions, builds formatted minutes in Confluence, and creates Jira action items — assigned and with due dates if mentioned.
detail: Every meeting produces two artifacts that never exist: structured minutes and actual action items with owners. Co-Work closes that gap. Paste the transcript or upload the doc. Claude reads it, identifies decisions (not just discussions), extracts action items with named owners and mentioned deadlines, builds formatted minutes in Confluence, and creates the Jira tickets. By the time the meeting ends, the follow-up infrastructure is already there.
prompt: Here's the transcript from our supplier quality review. Create Confluence minutes in the Manufacturing space and Jira tickets for each action item with owner and due date from the conversation.

title: Build supplier scorecards
blurb: Provide delivery, quality, and cost data across suppliers. Claude structures it into a supplier scorecard with rankings, trend notes, and a summary ready for your next vendor review.
detail: Supplier performance data usually lives in three places: a spreadsheet someone made six months ago, someone's inbox, and a verbal understanding that one supplier is "the difficult one." Co-Work consolidates it. Feed Claude your delivery, quality, and cost data. It structures everything into a proper supplier scorecard — ranked by performance, with trend commentary per vendor — formatted as a Confluence page you can bring to your next procurement review.
prompt: Here's 6 months of delivery and quality data for our top 8 suppliers. Build a supplier scorecard in Confluence with rankings, trend notes, and a recommendation on which relationships need attention.

title: Generate change order docs from parts lists
blurb: Feed Claude a parts list diff or BOM update. It drafts a structured ECO document — affected parts, change rationale, disposition instructions — formatted and ready to route.
detail: Engineering change orders need to communicate clearly to five different stakeholders who all want to know different things. Co-Work handles the document generation. Feed it a parts list diff, a BOM delta, or a summary of what changed. It drafts a structured ECO: affected part numbers, description of the change, rationale, disposition instructions for existing inventory, and a routing list for approvals. The kind of doc that usually takes an engineer 45 minutes from scratch.
prompt: Here's the BOM delta from REV C to REV D of the front suspension subassembly. Generate an ECO document covering affected parts, change description, rationale, and disposition of existing inventory.

title: Build BOM comparison tables
blurb: Provide two BOM exports. Claude compares them, highlights additions, removals, and quantity changes, and builds a clean comparison table in Confluence — linked to the source data.
detail: Two BOMs. One Excel export from yesterday, one from this morning. How different are they? Without Co-Work: open both, pivot table them, manually reconcile differences, make a table in Confluence, wonder if you missed something. With Co-Work: paste both, ask for a comparison. Claude produces a clean table — added parts, removed parts, quantity changes, description changes — structured and linked in Confluence in the format your team actually reads.
prompt: Here are two BOM exports for the canopy subassembly — last month's release and today's. Generate a comparison table in Confluence highlighting every delta with part number, change type, and quantities.

title: SSH in and run diagnostics autonomously
blurb: Point Claude Code at a server and it SSHes in, runs diagnostic commands, interprets the output, takes corrective steps, and reports back — without you typing a single command.
detail: Claude Code with SSH access is as close as you can get to having a sysadmin on call without actually paying a sysadmin. Point it at a server, describe what's wrong or what you want to know, and it connects, runs the relevant diagnostic commands, reads the output, decides what to check next based on what it finds, and gives you a plain-English report of what it discovered and what it did. Full audit trail. Zero manual command-typing required.
prompt: The Jenkins server has been running slow. SSH in, check CPU and memory utilization, look at the most resource-hungry processes, and tell me if anything is obviously wrong.

title: Analyze datasets end-to-end
blurb: Drop a CSV or point to a data source. Claude Code writes and runs the analysis, generates summary stats, creates charts, and produces a findings report — fully automated.
detail: Data analysis usually means: find the file, open Python or Excel, figure out the structure, write some code, fix the code, get the summary, export a chart, write it up. Claude Code handles every step. Drop the file path or describe the data source. Tell it what questions you want answered. It writes and runs the analysis code, interprets the outputs, generates summary statistics and charts, and produces a findings report — all in one go. You review the conclusions.
prompt: Analyze the quality defect CSV at /data/q2_defects.csv. Tell me which defect types are most common, which production lines they're from, and whether there's a trend over the 6-month period.

title: Build internal tools & automations
blurb: Have a repetitive multi-step process? Describe it once. Claude Code scopes, writes, tests, and deploys a script or small app to handle it — no ticket needed, no waiting on eng.
detail: Internal tools don't get built because nobody owns them and everyone's backlog is full. Claude Code changes the economics: you describe what you need, it scopes the implementation, builds it, tests it, and hands you something that works. A script that pulls from two APIs and emails a summary. A small dashboard that reads a shared folder. A bot that answers standard questions from a knowledge base. These aren't big projects anymore — they're afternoon tasks.

title: Nightly health-check Routine
